'''Judith Goslin Hall''' {{post-nominals|country=CAN|OC|FRSC|FCAHS}} (born July 3, 1939) is a [[pediatrician]], [[clinical geneticist]] and [[dysmorphology|dysmorphologist]] who is a dual citizen of the United States and Canada.{{citation needed lead|date=January 2017}}

== Early life and education ==
The daughter of a minister, Judith Goslin Hall was born on July 3, 1939, in [[Boston, Massachusetts]].<ref name="science.ca"/> She graduated from [[Garfield High School (Seattle)|Garfield High School]] in [[Seattle]] and then attended [[Wellesley College]] in Wellesley, Mass. from which she earned her [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in 1961.

She went to medical school in Seattle at the [[University of Washington]],<ref name="science.ca"/>  from which she received an [[Doctor of Medicine|MD]], from which she received an [[Doctor of Medicine|MD]]  degree in 1966.<ref name="science.ca"/> She was also awarded an [[Master of Science|MS]] degree in Genetics from the [[University of Washington]].<ref name="science.ca"/> She did her Pediatric training at [[Johns Hopkins Hospital]], and did her fellowships in [[Medical Genetics]] and [[Pediatric Endocrinology]].

== Career ==

In 1972, she returned to the University of Washington School of Medicine  and was given a joint appointment in the Departments of Pediatrics and Medicine as, successively, assistant, associate and full professor. She also gained additional depth of knowledge concerning [[congenital malformation]]s by working in Seattle with the pioneer [[dysmorphology|dysmorphologist]], [[David Weyhe Smith|David W. Smith]] (1926–1981).

In 1981, Hall was named professor of medical genetics at the [[University of British Columbia]]degree in 1966.<ref name="science.ca"/> and the Director of the Genetics Services for [[British Columbia]]. From 1990 to 2000, she was also Professor and head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of British Columbia and [[BC Children's Hospital]].<ref name="science.ca"/>

In 1988 she received a Killam Senior Fellowship for a sabbatical year at [[Oxford University]], UK. During 2001, she was a Distinguished Fellow at [[Christ's College, Cambridge|Christ's College]], [[Cambridge University]], UK.

From 1990 to 2000, she was Chair of Pediatrics at the University of British Columbia, being involved in paediatric education and paediatric physician resource planning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hall |first=Judith G. |date=August 2011 |title=Over the years, I hope I've learned a few things to pass along! |journal=Paediatrics & Child Health |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=387–388 |doi=10.1093/pch/16.7.387 |issn=1918-1485 |pmc=3200380 |pmid=22851888}}</ref>

In 2005, she became an [[Emeritus|Emerita]] Professor at the [[University of British Columbia]], engaged in Associations of Professors Emeriti (later the UBC Emeritus College), and served as the president in 2011–2012.

She described several forms of arthrogryposis and helped to define over 450 types.

== Awards ==
Hall has received a number of honors, including alumni awards from Garfield High School, [[Wellesley College]], the [[University of Washington School of Medicine]], and the [[University of British Columbia]]. In 1998, she was made an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]] as "a leader and world authority in both genetics and pediatrics" and having "contributed to the development of resources and services essential to coping with genetic illnesses" <ref name="science.ca">{{cite web|url=http://www.science.ca/scientists/scientistprofile.php?pID=368|title=science.ca: Judith G. Hall|work=science.ca|access-date=27 January 2017}}</ref> In 2011, she became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Canada]]. In 2015, Hall was inducted into the [[Canadian Medical Hall of Fame]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://cdnmedhall.org/inductees/dr-judith-g-hall-oc|title=Dr. Judith G. Hall, OC – Canadian Medical Hall of Fame|work=cdnmedhall.org|access-date=27 January 2017|archive-date=21 April 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170421204931/http://cdnmedhall.org/inductees/dr-judith-g-hall-oc}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[Canadian Academy of Health Sciences]].

Hall is quoted as saying, with regard to her recognition, that{{quote|To me, high achievement is not the number of publications but being a successful female in a world of professional men. And by that I mean caring more about peacemaking and nurturing the individual and the environment than success, winning, owning or directing.<ref name="science.ca"/>}}
